newsitem.title: UK: INTERVIEW-Boots sees BHI in profit soon.
newsitem.headline: INTERVIEW-Boots sees BHI in profit soon.

text.p: British retailer and pharmacist Boots Co Plc's ambitions to be a world player in branded medicines took a step forward on Thursday with the launch of its pain killer Nurofen in Russia.
The move into Russia is part of a major international marketing drive by Boots Healthcare International, which aims to bring the business into profit after some heavy investment.
BHI's strategy is focused on three key areas -- Nurofen, cough and cold remedy Strepsils and branded therapeutic skincare products -- all made by Boots.
Strepsils are already available in 130 countries and Nurofen in around 30 and BHI managing director Barry Clare said Boots was starting to dominate in these markets.
"We're achieving substantial growth rates in all of our major countries and our two core brands," he told Reuters in an interview.

Last year Boots subsidiary BHI spent 74 million pounds ($122 million) and this year could invest around 90 million pounds getting its products registered and marketed overseas. It launched Nurofen in France in February and has just got approval in Poland.
The high level of investment meant BHI made a loss last year of 8.2 million pounds.

But Clare is confident the business will soon start to show profits. "We're achieving more than double digit growth in the business so if the level of investment stays where it is...we will go into profit relatively soon."
The biggest single cost is the launch into new markets, which last year included Italy, Spain, Australia, the Czech and Slovak Republics.

In Eastern Europe, Clare said, it was crucial to be the first to market. Boots was first in the Czech Republic with Strepsils and got a 42 percent share in the first year. It was second in Poland and only got 17 percent. "It took us three years to get market leadership in Poland," he said.

BHI's strategy is to capitalise on the shift away from government- subsidised prescription drugs towards self medication via over-the-counter products. Clare believes European governments will increasingly see over-the-counter treatments as a safety valve to relieve the pressure of spiralling healthcare costs.
"All of Europe is beginning to understand the healthcare cost pressures...the market is being pushed towards self-medication."
Within the European Union BHI hopes gradual "harmonisation" will transform continental Europe's highly regulated and fragmented pharmacy business into a more UK-style over-the-counter market.
In Europe alone the market is worth an estimated 12 billion pounds.
Clare sees the newly formed European Medical Evaluation Agency making market access easier. From next year Boots will be able to apply to this body for pan-European product licences.
"It will dramatically reduce the length of time it is now taking us to get all of the countries to approve our products one by one," he said.
Once the brand is established in a market Boots hopes brand-extensions such as Nurofen Cold & Flu and Strepsil anasthetic throat sprays can drive profitability relatively quickly.
Boots already has the dominant otc dry skin treatment in Britain with E45 cream, but aims to expand in Europe via its purchase last year of French skincare specialist Laboratoires Lutsia.

Lutsia's brands, which include treatments for dry skin, acne and anti-ageing, have just been launched in Italy and Spain and later this year in Germany. BHI is also looking at bringing Lutsia products into Britain and eventually the Far East.
The gaps in BHI's plan for global domination include, however, the United States, where Nurofen was licensed to American Home Products in 1983 and sells under the brand Advil.

BHI would still like to find a way into the U.S., but Clare acknowledged it would be difficult at this stage in such a fiercely competitive market. Although he said there might be scope as BHI develops new products.
The other key market where Nurofen is not on sale is Germany, where Boots has been searching long and hard to make an over-the-counter acquisition.
Clare said the problem Boots faced was that the firms were all private and none wanted to sell.
He said it might already be too late to launch conventional Nurofen in Germany, but the more advanced versions such as the children's syrup might be more attractive.

BHI is prepared to consider alliances or partnerships and has found several of the OTC firms willing to talk. Clare said the addition of the Lutsia skincare range to BHI's war chest could help get them into Germany.
"If you like we've been massing the BHI army on the borders and now we're ready to invade."
